export const meta = {
  name: 'audit-certificate-console',
  description: 'Independent adversarial audit of the certificate admin console against its spec: 9 read-only auditors, one per risk area, each must reproduce what it reports',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Audit', detail: 'one independent auditor per risk area; findings need concrete reproduction' },
  ],
}

const SPEC = [
  "# Project Spec: Multi-Tenant Certificate Admin Console",
  "",
  "Build an internal admin console for a multi-tenant training platform where tenant admins review course completions, issue certificates, revoke them, and export certificate data.",
  "",
  "## 1. Tech Stack & Constraints",
  "- **Backend**: Go, Python, or Node.js with a mainstream framework. Use SQLite, MySQL, or PostgreSQL (persistent storage required, no in-memory-only DB).",
  "- **Frontend**: Vue 3 or React (Vite optional).",
  "- **Startup**: Provide one documented command that installs/uses declared dependencies, initializes demo data, and starts the full app. Optionally provide a second command to run verification tests.",
  "- **Actor Context**: No login UI needed. Seed one admin per tenant and identify the actor via an HTTP header or token (e.g., `X-Actor-Email`).",
  "- **Scope Control**: Do not add production auth, cloud deployment, notifications, or unrelated features. Prioritize core behavioral correctness over visual polish.",
  "",
  "## 2. Seed / Demo Data Requirements",
  "- Two tenants:",
  "  - `East` with timezone `Australia/Sydney`",
  "  - `West` with timezone `Australia/Perth`",
  "- Two admins (each bound strictly to their own tenant):",
  "  - `alice@east.test` -> `East`",
  "  - `bob@west.test` -> `West`",
  "- Both tenants must have a course titled `Safety 101` and a learner named `Alex Lee`, including completed, incomplete, and already-certified enrollments.",
  "- Provide a separate CLI command or script to generate 100,000 certificate rows for one tenant (`East`) without altering the default quick-start dataset.",
  "",
  "## 3. Core Workflows",
  "1. **Certificate List**: Switch/select actor, search by learner name or serial number, paginate, and sort. Show loading, empty, and error states.",
  "2. **Bulk Issue**: Choose a course and issue certificates to all eligible (completed, not yet certified) learners. Prevent duplicate UI submissions and show operation status. Return per-learner outcomes: `issued`, `skipped` (with reason), or `failed`.",
  "3. **Certificate Detail & Revocation**: Display serial number, course, learner, tenant-local issue date, and status. Support revocation with UI confirmation. Write audit logs for both issuance and revocation.",
  "4. **CSV Export**: Export columns: learner name, course title, serial number, and tenant-local issue date. Preserve active search and sort filters. Must handle 100,000-row exports efficiently without blocking concurrent reads.",
  "",
  "## 4. Acceptance Criteria (Must Pass)",
  "- **A1 (Tenant Isolation)**: If `bob@west.test` attempts to access `East` data via list, detail, bulk issue, or export endpoints, only `West` data is accessible. Cross-tenant detail requests must return `404`. Cross-tenant bulk issue must be rejected without creating certificates or audit events.",
  "- **A2 (Retry Safety / Idempotency)**: Sequential and concurrent identical bulk-issue requests from Alice with the same `Idempotency-Key` must execute as one logical operation. Each eligible learner gets at most 1 certificate and 1 audit event. All callers receive the same logical outcome.",
  "- **A3 (Idempotency Key Misuse)**: If Alice reuses an `Idempotency-Key` with a different course ID or payload, return `409 Conflict` without executing a second operation or overwriting the first result.",
  "- **A4 (Learner Outcomes)**: Bulk issuing a course with completed, incomplete, and already-certified learners only issues to eligible learners and skips the rest with clear reasons.",
  "- **A5 (DST & Local Date)**: A certificate with UTC timestamp `2026-01-10T13:30:00Z` must display as `2026-01-11 00:30` for `East` (`Australia/Sydney`) and `2026-01-10 21:30` for `West` (`Australia/Perth`). List sorting and CSV export must use the tenant-local calendar date.",
  "- **A6 (Export Scalability & Determinism)**: With 100,000 `East` certificates (including duplicate sort values), running a filtered and sorted CSV export twice must complete each within 60 seconds, return exact matching rows in deterministic order (use a tie-breaker like `id` for equal sort keys), and not block concurrent certificate list API requests during export.",
  "- **A7 (Revocation Audit)**: Revoking a valid certificate changes its status and writes 1 audit event. Repeating the revoke request is idempotent and does not create duplicate audit events.",
].join("\n")

const PROJECT = "/home/user/cert-admin-console"
const AUDIT_ROOT = "/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/61a877e9-483e-575a-b7cf-c5b8e94decb9/scratchpad/audit"

const AREAS = [
  {
    key: "tenant-isolation",
    portBase: 4100,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: tenant isolation (acceptance criterion A1) and hostile or malformed input on every endpoint.",
      "- Enumerate every route in backend/src/app.js and every SQL statement in backend/src/services and backend/src/db. For each, establish where the tenant restriction comes from and whether any path can read or write another tenant's rows.",
      "- Attack it over HTTP as bob@west.test against East data and as alice@east.test against West data: list, detail, revoke, bulk issue, export, course roster, bulk-operation lookups, audit events. Use ids of the other tenant, guessed parameters (tenant, tenantId, ...), repeated / array-style / object-style query parameters, every parameter alias the code accepts, LIKE wildcards, SQL metacharacters in q / sort / order / status, numeric edge cases in ids and paging, and odd X-Actor-Email values (case, whitespace, comma lists, duplicated header, missing, unknown).",
      "- For 'must be rejected without creating certificates or audit events', compare row counts in the SQLite file before and after (certificates, audit_events, bulk_issue_operations).",
      "- Check that a cross-tenant 404 is indistinguishable from a plain not-found 404 and that no error body, response header or CSV leaks data of another tenant.",
      "- Idempotency keys across tenants: can Bob replay, collide with, block or observe an operation Alice executed with the same key?",
      "- Also probe general input robustness on each endpoint: malformed JSON, wrong content types, oversized bodies, unsupported methods, malformed URL encodings, very long values. A 5xx answer, a hang or a crashed server is a finding.",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "idempotency-concurrency",
    portBase: 4200,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: retry safety and idempotency-key misuse for bulk issue (acceptance criteria A2 and A3), including the database transaction layer they rely on.",
      "- Read backend/src/services/bulkIssue.js, backend/src/services/ledger.js, backend/src/db/sqlite.js and backend/src/db/schema.js closely. Look for any interleaving, error path or partial failure in which an eligible learner could get two certificates or two issuance audit events, an operation could execute twice, a retry could receive a different outcome, or a failed transaction could leave partial writes or a broken connection state (nested savepoints, rollback or commit failures, exceptions thrown at each step).",
      "- Demonstrate behaviour with real requests: sequential retries; many truly concurrent identical requests (write a Node script; also start a second server process on the same DB_PATH and split the requests across both processes); the same key with a different course id; the same key with a changed payload (extra field, different value types, different formatting or key order, empty or missing body, invalid JSON); a key first used on a rejected request and then reused; odd key values (empty, whitespace, very long, non-ASCII, repeated header); requests without a key; a client that disconnects before reading the response and then retries; a replay after the data changed (for example a certificate issued by the operation was revoked afterwards).",
      "- Verify 'all callers receive the same logical outcome' literally: status code, body, and which requests report themselves as replays.",
      "- Verify 'without executing a second operation or overwriting the first result' for A3 by inspecting the database rows as well as the responses.",
      "- Consider a long-running writer in another process (for example the 100,000-row generator CLI running while bulk-issue requests arrive at the server): do requests fail, hang, double-execute, or return errors that a retrying client would mishandle?",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "outcomes-revocation-audit",
    portBase: 4300,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: per-learner outcomes of bulk issue (A4) and certificate revocation with its audit trail (A7), plus the audit log in general (spec: 'Write audit logs for both issuance and revocation').",
      "- For every seeded course in both tenants, predict from the seed data (backend/src/db/seed.js or the database itself) what a bulk issue must do for each learner, then run it and compare: issued only to completed-and-not-yet-certified learners, everyone else skipped with a clear reason, summary counts consistent with the per-learner list, certificates / serial numbers / audit events actually present and correct in the database.",
      "- Check that the roster preview endpoint (GET /api/courses/:id/enrollments) and the real operation agree for every learner, including pagination and totals of the roster.",
      "- Find a way to make issuance fail for one learner (think about what data could make the insert fail) and observe whether the others are still processed, what is reported, and whether partial writes remain.",
      "- Revocation: a valid revoke changes status and writes exactly one audit event; repeats are idempotent with no extra event; many concurrent revokes of one certificate (also across two server processes sharing one database file) still give one event; revoke with and without a body, with invalid input, of unknown ids; what the list, detail, export and a later bulk issue show afterwards.",
      "- Audit integrity as an invariant: after a long random sequence of bulk issues and revokes (write a script), every certificate has exactly one certificate.issued event and every revoked certificate exactly one certificate.revoked event, with correct actor, tenant and timestamps; no audit event exists for rejected, replayed or no-op requests. Also exercise GET /api/audit-events (filters, paging, invalid parameters) and the operation history endpoints.",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "time-dst",
    portBase: 4400,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: time zones, daylight saving and tenant-local dates (acceptance criterion A5).",
      "- Verify the reference case in the running app for both tenants in the list, the detail and the CSV: UTC 2026-01-10T13:30:00Z must display as 2026-01-11 00:30 for East (Australia/Sydney) and 2026-01-10 21:30 for West (Australia/Perth).",
      "- Check the conversion code (backend/src/lib/time.js and every caller) against an independent implementation (Python zoneinfo) over thousands of instants: around both Sydney DST transitions of several years, midnight boundaries, year boundaries, and other zones (half-hour offsets, zones west of UTC). Include the stored issued_local_date column of every certificate after running the 100,000-row generator in your copy.",
      "- 'List sorting and CSV export must use the tenant-local calendar date': build adversarial data in a database copy (certificates just before and after local midnight, on both sides of DST changes, same UTC date but different local dates and vice versa, inserted in an order that differs from chronological order) and check the order returned by the list and by the export for sort=issued in both directions, in both tenants, against your own computation.",
      "- Check everything else that prints or derives a date: revocation times, audit event times, roster completion times, bulk-issue results, export file name, operation history. Look for any use of the server's own time zone or of the UTC date where the tenant-local date is required: run the server under different TZ environment values (for example TZ=America/New_York and TZ=Asia/Tokyo) and compare outputs.",
      "- Frontend: confirm the UI shows the tenant-local strings regardless of the browser's time zone (run Playwright with timezoneId set to a zone far from Australia) in the list, the detail drawer and bulk-issue results. You need the UI built in your copy for this (npm run build, or npm start).",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "export-scale",
    portBase: 4500,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: export scalability and determinism on 100,000 East certificates (acceptance criterion A6) and the generator CLI that produces them (spec section 2, last bullet).",
      "- In your copy, take a full dump of the freshly seeded database, run the documented generator command, and verify independently (Python sqlite3): exactly 100,000 certificate rows were added for East, nothing was added for West, every quick-start row is unchanged, and the generated data really contains duplicate sort values for every sortable column. Exercise the generator's options and edge cases (re-run, --count, --clear, --db, bad arguments, running it while the server is up and serving requests).",
      "- For several filtered + sorted exports (each sort key, both directions, with search text, with the status filter, with characters special to LIKE or to CSV): run each twice, time it, compare bytes, parse with Python's csv module, and compare the row set and the exact order with an independent computation from the database (sort key plus tie-breaker). Check the CSV against the spec's column list and against the list API page by page.",
      "- 'Not block concurrent certificate list API requests during export': measure list latency without any export, then while exports are streaming (several at once, and with a client that reads slowly or stalls), and compare. Poll a cheap endpoint during exports to find the longest event-loop stall. Explain any stall you find from the code (backend/src/services/certificates.js, backend/src/app.js).",
      "- Resource behaviour: abort many downloads mid-way and check the server process for leaked file descriptors / database connections (/proc/<pid>/fd) and for memory growth; run 20+ exports concurrently; check that writes (bulk issue, revoke) during an export succeed and whether the export is a consistent snapshot.",
      "- Pagination determinism on equal sort keys (no row repeated or skipped across pages), deep pages, a page beyond the end, and consistency between the reported total and the rows returned.",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "frontend-ui",
    portBase: 4600,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: the React frontend (frontend/src) and the four UI workflows of spec section 3, tested in a real browser with Playwright.",
      "- Build and start your copy (PORT=<your port> npm start, or npm run build followed by the server). Drive the UI as a user would and as an impatient user would. Check the browser console for errors and warnings throughout.",
      "- Certificate list: actor switch, search by learner name and by serial number, pagination, sorting, loading / empty / error states (use page.route to delay, fail or corrupt API responses). Look for races: out-of-order responses while typing, switching actor while requests are in flight (does data of the previous tenant ever render under the new one?), stale detail drawers, page numbers that outlive a filter change.",
      "- Bulk issue: choosing a course, duplicate-submission prevention (double click, Enter key, clicking during the request, changing course mid-flight), operation status display, per-learner outcomes, behaviour when the response is lost and the request is retried (is the same Idempotency-Key reused? when is a new one generated?), behaviour on 4xx and 5xx answers.",
      "- Detail and revocation: all required fields shown, tenant-local issue date, status; the confirmation step (cancel, Escape, backdrop click, double click on confirm, failure of the request); list refresh afterwards; deep links to a certificate of the other tenant; browser back / forward and reload.",
      "- CSV export from the UI: does the downloaded file contain exactly the rows and order of the active search, status filter and sort (also when the user types and immediately clicks Export, and after changing the sort through the column headers)? Behaviour for large exports and for failures.",
      "- Use the generator CLI in your copy (npm run generate:east) for a 100,000-row dataset when checking pagination and export. Also read the components for logic errors a browser run might not hit (stale closures, missing cleanup, state not reset between actors, unhandled promise rejections).",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "startup-docs-spec",
    portBase: 4700,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: the first-run experience, the documentation, and literal compliance with spec sections 1 and 2.",
      "- Simulate a fresh checkout: instead of the plain cp in ground rule 2, copy the project WITHOUT node_modules, without frontend/dist and without any data/*.sqlite* files, then run the one documented start command with your PORT and nothing else. It must install, initialise demo data and start the full app (UI and API). Then run the documented test command. Record what happened, how long it took, and anything a first-time evaluator would trip over (warnings, ports, confusing output).",
      "- Execute every command and every curl example in README.md exactly as written (adapting only the port) against a fresh database, in order, and compare with what the README says will happen. Check every factual claim in the README that you can test: ids, counts, file layout, behaviours, numbers, environment variables, troubleshooting advice, the claimed fallback when the native SQLite module is unavailable (simulate that in your copy), restart persistence (data survives a restart, nothing is seeded twice), reset while the server is running, development mode.",
      "- Check the seed data against spec section 2 word by word (tenants and time zones, admins bound strictly to their own tenant, the Safety 101 course and the learner Alex Lee in both tenants, completed / incomplete / already-certified enrollments), and the generator requirement.",
      "- Check the section 1 constraints: stack, persistent storage (not in-memory only), actor identification, and scope control (anything that looks like production auth, deployment, notifications or unrelated features).",
      "- Check repository hygiene: package.json scripts and engines, lockfile in sync (npm ci), .gitignore, stray files, and whether the documented commands would plausibly work on macOS and Windows (flag shell-specific constructs).",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "test-suite-quality",
    portBase: 4800,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: the verification tests (backend/test) - are they real evidence for A1-A7?",
      "- Map each acceptance criterion to the tests that claim to verify it and judge whether a violation would actually be caught.",
      "- Mutation testing in your copy: introduce at least 20 small, realistic defects one at a time into the backend (examples: remove the tenant predicate from one query at a time; skip or duplicate an audit insert; compare the idempotency fingerprint incorrectly or ignore it; scope the key lookup too broadly; drop the id tie-breaker from one ordering; sort by the UTC date; let a revoked certificate be re-issued; remove the status guard from revoke; break LIKE escaping; off-by-one in paging; swap CSV columns; change the CSV date format; make bulk issue non-atomic; return a different body on replay). Run the relevant test file(s) after each mutation and restore the file afterwards. Report every mutant that SURVIVES, with the exact diff and a concrete test that would kill it.",
      "- Run the whole suite at least three times and report flaky or timing-sensitive tests, tests that depend on execution order or on the current date / time zone of the machine (try TZ=America/New_York and TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati), and tests that would pass vacuously.",
      "- Note acceptance-relevant behaviour that has no test at all.",
    ],
  },
  {
    key: "backend-review-fuzz",
    portBase: 4900,
    focus: [
      "YOUR AREA: line-by-line review of the backend source (backend/src, backend/scripts, scripts/) for defects not tied to a single acceptance criterion, plus fuzzing of the running server.",
      "- Read every file. Look for logic errors, wrong edge-case handling (parameter parsing limits and aliases, id parsing, pagination arithmetic, empty results), error paths that leave state behind, promises that can reject unhandled, streams or database connections that can leak, places where the process could crash or hang, misleading error mapping, and mismatches between comments / README and actual behaviour.",
      "- Pay particular attention to backend/src/app.js (body parsing is configured to treat every content type as JSON; the streaming export route and its cleanup; the static file fallback; the error handler), backend/src/db/sqlite.js (two interchangeable drivers: run the server and the test suite with SQLITE_DRIVER=node and with SQLITE_DRIVER=better-sqlite3 and look for behavioural differences), and backend/scripts (argument handling, running against a live server, reset).",
      "- Fuzz the HTTP surface of a running instance with a script: random and boundary values for every parameter and header, malformed percent-encodings, NUL and control characters, huge values, unexpected JSON types and deep nesting, wrong methods, abrupt disconnects during request bodies and during streamed responses, many parallel connections. Any 5xx answer, unhandled exception in the server log, crash, hang or corrupted response is a finding; so is any input that is accepted but produces a wrong result.",
    ],
  },
]

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    summary: { type: 'string', description: 'Two or three sentences: what you covered and your overall verdict for this area.' },
    checksPerformed: {
      type: 'array',
      items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'Concrete checks you ran and their result, including the ones that passed.',
    },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          title: { type: 'string' },
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['critical', 'major', 'minor', 'nit'] },
          category: {
            type: 'string',
            enum: ['spec-violation', 'bug', 'robustness', 'data-integrity', 'performance', 'docs', 'test-gap', 'ux', 'spec-interpretation'],
          },
          criterion: { type: 'string', description: 'A1..A7, or the spec section, or "general".' },
          location: { type: 'string', description: 'file:line (or several) in the deliverable.' },
          description: { type: 'string', description: 'What is wrong and why it matters.' },
          reproduction: { type: 'string', description: 'Exact commands / requests / script and the observed output.' },
          expected: { type: 'string', description: 'What the spec or README requires instead.' },
          reproduced: { type: 'boolean', description: 'true only if you observed the faulty behaviour yourself.' },
          suggestedFix: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['title', 'severity', 'category', 'criterion', 'description', 'reproduction', 'reproduced'],
      },
    },
  },
  required: ['summary', 'checksPerformed', 'findings'],
}

function buildPrompt(area) {
  const workdir = AUDIT_ROOT + "/" + area.key
  return [
    "You are an independent auditor. A software deliverable was built to the specification below, and its author claims it meets every acceptance criterion. Your job is to find where that claim is false or fragile within your assigned area. You did not write this code and owe it no benefit of the doubt - but you must not report anything you have not actually checked.",
    "",
    "=== SPECIFICATION (verbatim from the client) ===",
    SPEC,
    "=== END OF SPECIFICATION ===",
    "",
    "THE DELIVERABLE",
    "- Source tree: " + PROJECT + " - a Node.js / Express 5 + SQLite backend in backend/, a React + Vite frontend in frontend/, verification tests in backend/test, and README.md, which documents the commands, the HTTP API and the design decisions.",
    "- Read README.md first, then the code relevant to your area.",
    "",
    "GROUND RULES (several auditors work on this machine at the same time)",
    "1. " + PROJECT + " is READ-ONLY for you. Never create, edit, build or run anything inside it: no npm start / test / install there, no database files there.",
    "2. Work only in your private directory " + workdir + ". Start with:  mkdir -p " + workdir + " && cp -a " + PROJECT + " " + workdir + "/app   (node_modules is included, so no install is needed; frontend/dist is not built: `npm run build` in your copy builds the UI, and `npm start` in your copy installs, builds and serves everything).",
    "3. Network ports: use only ports " + area.portBase + " to " + (area.portBase + 49) + " (for example `PORT=" + area.portBase + " npm start` in your copy, or `PORT=" + (area.portBase + 1) + " DB_PATH=/some/file.sqlite node backend/src/server.js`). The test suite picks free ports by itself.",
    "4. Never use pkill or killall, and never kill a process you did not start: other auditors run identically named processes. Record the PIDs you start and kill exactly those. Before you finish, stop every process you started.",
    "5. The machine has 4 cores that you share with another auditor running concurrently, so absolute timings are noisy. Report a performance problem only if it is structural (you can explain the mechanism from the code) or reproduces with a wide margin.",
    "6. Available tools: node 22, npm, curl, python3 (its sqlite3, csv and zoneinfo modules are handy for independent checks of the SQLite file and of CSV output), and Playwright with Chromium (require('playwright') works from any directory and chromium.launch() needs no options; do not install anything for it).",
    "7. The databases are SQLite files in WAL mode. To inspect one while a server is running, open it read-only from Python or from Node in your copy.",
    "",
    area.focus.join("\n"),
    "",
    "WHAT COUNTS AS A FINDING",
    "- A violation of the specification or of an acceptance criterion; wrong results; data written when it must not be (or not written when it must be); a crash, hang, leak or unhandled error with a concrete trigger; a documented command or README claim that does not hold; a UI workflow that misbehaves; a verification test that would not catch the defect it claims to guard against.",
    "- Not findings: style preferences; features the spec does not ask for (it says to avoid unrelated features); production concerns the spec excludes (real authentication, deployment); design decisions that the README documents - unless such a decision contradicts the wording of the spec, in which case report it under category spec-interpretation and quote the sentence it conflicts with.",
    "- Every finding needs evidence: the exact commands, requests or script you ran and what you observed, versus what the spec or the README requires. If you are convinced something is wrong but could not demonstrate it, you may report it with reproduced=false and say exactly what you tried; keep such items few and well argued.",
    "- An empty findings list is a valid and respectable result. Do not pad the list. Do not soften or inflate severity: critical = an acceptance criterion fails; major = a spec requirement or core workflow is partly broken, or data integrity is at risk; minor = a real but limited defect; nit = cosmetic or documentation inaccuracy.",
    "- Stay in your area (other auditors cover the rest), but do report anything serious you stumble on elsewhere.",
    "",
    "Be thorough within your area: work through the whole checklist above, then try the ideas of your own that seem most likely to break things. In checksPerformed, list concretely what you verified - including what turned out to be correct; that coverage record matters as much as the findings.",
  ].join("\n")
}

phase('Audit')
const results = await parallel(
  AREAS.map((area) => () =>
    agent(buildPrompt(area), { label: 'audit:' + area.key, phase: 'Audit', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA }).then((r) =>
      r ? { area: area.key, summary: r.summary, checksPerformed: r.checksPerformed, findings: r.findings } : null,
    ),
  ),
)

const completed = results.filter(Boolean)
const missing = AREAS.filter((area, i) => !results[i]).map((area) => area.key)
if (missing.length > 0) log('No result from: ' + missing.join(', '))
const total = completed.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.findings.length, 0)
log(completed.length + '/' + AREAS.length + ' auditors reported, ' + total + ' findings in total')

return { completed, missing }

completed.summary: Tenant isolation (A1) held under every attack I ran: as bob@west.test against East and as alice@east.test against West, on list, detail, revoke, bulk issue, export, roster, bulk-operation lookups and audit events, I found no way to read or write another tenant's rows. Cross-tenant 404s are byte-identical to plain not-found 404s, rejected cross-tenant writes leave every table unchanged, and idempotency keys cannot be replayed, collided with, blocked or observed across tenants. The four findings are outside A1's pass/fail: two deterministic 500s from crafted input, unsanitised NUL / unpaired-surrogate text, and one overstated README claim about schema-level isolation. The server never crashed or hung, and all four servers I started are stopped.
checksPerformed: Code review: enumerated all 13 API routes plus the catch-all and static/SPA fallback in backend/src/app.js, and every SQL statement in backend/src/services and backend/src/db. Every runtime statement takes tenant_id from the actor record resolved from X-Actor-Email. The two without a tenant predicate (ledger.js:109 SELECT after a tenant-scoped UPDATE; bulkIssue.js:178 UPDATE by the rowid just inserted) cannot be reached with a foreign id. No test hook or env switch is reachable over HTTP.
Ran the deliverable's own suite in my private copy (TMPDIR inside my directory): 77/77 pass in 14 s; the A1 and actor-context subset passes 10/10.

List as Bob: 59 query variants (guessed tenant/tenantId/tenant_id/actor parameters, array- and object-style parameters, LIKE wildcards, SQL metacharacters, every alias: search, sortBy, dir, direction, sortOrder, page_size, per_page, limit). Every 200 contained only WEST- rows; q=EAST, q=%25 and q=_ returned 0 rows. 11 variants as Alice returned only EAST- rows.

Detail: Bob on East ids 1-7 and newly issued 12, 13, Alice on West ids 8-11: all 404, with status, all headers except Date, and body byte-identical to the 404 for id 999999. 44 odd id spellings (01, +1, 1.0, 1e0, %31, encoded slashes, 16+ digits, fullwidth digits, SQL fragments) gave 404 or 400, never 5xx and never a foreign row.

Cross-tenant revoke: Bob on certificates 1-7 with 4 variants each (reason, no body, tenantId in body and query, X-Tenant-Id header) and Alice on 8-11: all 404 identical to missing. A SHA-256 digest over every row of all 8 tables was unchanged; PUT/PATCH/DELETE/OPTIONS on those paths gave 404.

Cross-tenant bulk issue: 20 variants as Bob against East courses 1-3 (courseId as number or string, course_id alias, tenant fields in body, query and headers, duplicate JSON keys, __proto__, with and without Idempotency-Key, repeated) and Alice against courses 4-6. All 404, byte-identical to the unknown-course 404; counts of certificates, audit_events and bulk_issue_operations and the full-table digest were unchanged. 20 invalid body shapes gave 400 or 404 with nothing written.

findings.title: List and export return 500 for sort=constructor: an inherited Object.prototype key passes the sort whitelist
findings.description: The sort whitelist SORT_ALIASES is a plain object literal. After lower-casing and stripping non-letters, the value "constructor" resolves to the inherited Object function, which is truthy, so the `if (!sort)` check passes. With an explicit order, or the `-` prefix that implies desc, the request proceeds and `SORTS[sort]` is undefined, so orderBy() throws a TypeError and the client gets 500 internal_error on both the list and the CSV export. Without an order the caller gets a misleading 400 about "order" instead of "sort". Every spelling that normalises to "constructor" works (Constructor, con-struc_tor, the sortBy alias), on both SQLite drivers. No data is exposed, the read transaction is rolled back and the server keeps running. The effect is that a client input error is reported as a server fault with a stack trace logged per request, contradicting the comment at certificates.js:69 that unknown values are rejected. The suite's 'rejects malformed list parameters with a 400' test only tries sort=password.
findings.expected: 400 invalid_request with '"sort" must be one of: issued, learner, course, serial, status', as for any other unknown sort value.
findings.reproduction:
In a private copy: PORT=4122 DB_PATH=<private>/ui.sqlite node backend/src/server.js, then with -H 'X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test':

curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates?sort=-constructor'
-> 500 {"error":{"code":"internal_error","message":"Unexpected server error"}}
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates?sort=constructor&order=asc'  -> 500 (same body)
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates/export.csv?sort=constructor&order=asc'  -> 500 (same body)
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates?sort=constructor'
-> 400 {"error":{"code":"invalid_request","message":"\"order\" must be \"asc\" or \"desc\""}}
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates?sort=password&order=asc'
-> 400 '"sort" must be one of: issued, learner, course, serial, status' (the correct behaviour)

Server log: [error] GET /api/certificates?sort=-constructor: TypeError: SORTS[sort] is not a function at orderBy (backend/src/services/certificates.js:119:49). Also 500 for sort=Constructor&order=asc, sort=con-struc_tor&order=asc, sortBy=-constructor, and with SQLITE_DRIVER=node.
findings.suggestedFix: Look the alias up with Object.hasOwn(SORT_ALIASES, key), or build SORT_ALIASES, SORTS, SORT_INDEXES and DEFAULT_ORDER as Maps or null-prototype objects, and add sort=constructor to the malformed-parameter test.

findings.title: POST /api/bulk-issues returns 500 for a JSON body nested about 3,000 levels deep: stack overflow in fingerprinting before validation
findings.location: /home/user/cert-admin-console/backend/src/lib/fingerprint.js:4-12 (recursive canonicalJson); /home/user/cert-admin-console/backend/src/services/bulkIssue.js:62 (fingerprint computed before the body is validated)
findings.description: bulkIssue() fingerprints the whole request body with the recursive canonicalJson() before checking that the body is an object with a courseId. JSON.parse accepts very deep nesting, but canonicalJson overflows the call stack at about 2,950 nested arrays (a 5.9 KB body) or about 2,250 nested objects (13.5 KB), far below the 100 kb body limit. The RangeError falls through to the generic handler and the caller gets 500 internal_error instead of a 400. This also hits a request that is otherwise valid: a correct courseId and Idempotency-Key plus one deeply nested extra member is answered 500. Nothing is written, because the error occurs before the transaction, and the server keeps running. Each such request logs a stack trace, and the README and UI treat 5xx on this endpoint as 'outcome unknown, retry safely', which is misleading for a deterministic input error.
findings.expected: 400 invalid_request (or invalid_json) for a body the server will not process; no input within the documented 100 kb limit should produce a 5xx.
findings.reproduction:
Server as above, as bob@west.test:

python3 -c "print('['*3000+']'*3000)" | curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/bulk-issues
-> 500 {"error":{"code":"internal_error","message":"Unexpected server error"}}

python3 -c "print('{\"courseId\": 4, \"x\": ' + '['*3000+']'*3000 + '}')" | curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: deep-1' --data-binary @- http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/bulk-issues
-> 500 (same body); afterwards SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bulk_issue_operations WHERE idempotency_key='deep-1' returns 0.

Depth 1000 gives the expected 400 'Request body must be a JSON object such as {"courseId": 1}'. Bisected thresholds: arrays last OK about 2937, first 500 about 2952; objects last OK about 2234, first 500 about 2250. Server log: [error] POST /api/bulk-issues: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded at canonicalJson (backend/src/lib/fingerprint.js:4:30) at Array.map at canonicalJson (fingerprint.js:6:46). Same result with SQLITE_DRIVER=node.
findings.suggestedFix: Validate the body shape first and fingerprint only the validated fields (for example {courseId}), or make canonicalJson iterative or depth-limited and map the overflow to a 400.

findings.title: NUL characters and unpaired surrogates are accepted in free text: revocation reason is stored as invalid UTF-8, and a NUL in q changes what the search matches
findings.location: /home/user/cert-admin-console/backend/src/services/certificates.js:229-238 (parseRevocationReason: only type and length are checked); /home/user/cert-admin-console/backend/src/lib/params.js:5-15 and certificates.js:105-111 (q goes into the LIKE pattern unchecked)
findings.description:
This needs a direct API call; the UI cannot produce these characters, and only the caller's own tenant is affected.

(a) Revocation reason. The only persisted free-text input accepts U+0000 and unpaired surrogates. With the default better-sqlite3 driver the reason is stored in the STRICT TEXT column certificates.revocation_reason as bytes 'a\x00b \xed\xa0\x80 end', that is, an embedded NUL plus an invalid UTF-8 sequence. SQL length() then reports 1, and a standard client (Python sqlite3) can no longer read the certificates table. The API itself returns two different versions of the same reason: revocationReason shows three U+FFFD characters while auditEvents[].details.reason shows the original \ud800. With the node:sqlite fallback the stored bytes are valid but the API returns the reason cut at the NUL ("a").

(b) Search. SQLite's LIKE stops at a NUL in the bound pattern, so q=<text>%00<anything> becomes 'ends with <text>' and q=%00 matches every row of the tenant, in both list and export. The tenant predicate is unaffected.
findings.expected: 400 invalid_request for text containing U+0000 or unpaired surrogates (or strip them) before it reaches SQL, so that stored values are valid UTF-8, both copies of the reason agree, and a search never matches rows that do not contain the search text.
findings.reproduction:
Server as above, as bob@west.test (certificate 9 is Bob's own, active):

curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"reason":"a\u0000b \ud800 end"}' http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates/9/revoke
-> 200, "status":"revoked", revocationReason = 'a\x00b ��� end', but auditEvents[-1].details.reason = 'a\x00b \ud800 end'

python3: sqlite3.connect('file:ui.sqlite?mode=ro', uri=True).execute('SELECT * FROM certificates').fetchall()
-> OperationalError: Could not decode to UTF-8 column 'revocation_reason' with text 'a'
With text_factory=bytes: SELECT revocation_reason, length(revocation_reason) FROM certificates WHERE id=9 -> (b'a\x00b \xed\xa0\x80 end', 1)

With SQLITE_DRIVER=node, the same request on certificate 11 stores b'a\x00b \xef\xbf\xbd end' and the API returns "revocationReason":"a".

Search: curl -s -H 'X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test' 'http://127.0.0.1:4122/api/certificates?q=Lee%00zzzz' -> total 1 ['Alex Lee'], echoed q 'Lee\x00zzzz'; q=Leezzzz -> total 0. q=%00 -> total 4 (all of Bob's rows; 100,007 for Alice on the load database). export.csv?q=%00 returns all rows too.
findings.suggestedFix: In queryString() and parseRevocationReason(), reject strings that contain \u0000 (ideally all C0 control characters) or fail String.prototype.isWellFormed() with a 400, and add cases to the validation tests.

findings.title: README overstates schema-level isolation: four foreign keys are single-column, so a West audit event can reference an East certificate
findings.description: README section 6 (A1 row) says: 'On top of that the schema uses composite (id, tenant_id) foreign keys, so cross-tenant rows cannot even be inserted.' That holds for references to courses, learners and admins, but four references are plain single-column keys: certificates.enrollment_id, certificates.bulk_operation_id, audit_events.certificate_id and audit_events.bulk_operation_id. With foreign_keys=ON the database accepts a West audit event pointing at an East certificate or East bulk operation, and a West certificate pointing at an East enrollment or bulk operation. No HTTP path produces such rows, so this is a gap in the claimed second line of defence only, most relevant for audit_events, which A1 names explicitly. The unit test 'enforces tenant boundaries in the schema itself' covers only the course/learner pair for enrollments and certificates, so it does not notice.
findings.expected: Either the claim is narrowed to course, learner and admin references, or the remaining references become composite (UNIQUE (id, tenant_id) on certificates, enrollments and bulk_issue_operations, with composite foreign keys from audit_events and certificates) and the unit test covers them.
findings.reproduction:
On a private backup copy of a seeded database (after one East bulk issue so operation 1 exists), Python sqlite3 with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; West = tenant 2, East ids: certificate 1, enrollment 1, bulk operation 1:

ACCEPTED: INSERT INTO audit_events (tenant_id, actor_admin_id, actor_email, action, certificate_id, details, created_at) VALUES (2, 2, 'bob@west.test', 'certificate.revoked', 1, '{}', ...)
ACCEPTED: audit_events with tenant_id 2, certificate_id 9 (West), bulk_operation_id 1 (East)
ACCEPTED: audit_events with tenant_id 2, actor_admin_id NULL, actor_email 'alice@east.test', certificate_id 1 (East)
ACCEPTED: certificates with tenant_id 2, course 6, learner 9 (both West), enrollment_id 1 (East)
ACCEPTED: certificates with tenant_id 2, course 6, learner 12 (both West), bulk_operation_id 1 (East)

For contrast, 7 other mixed-tenant inserts fail with 'FOREIGN KEY constraint failed': certificate with East course, East learner or East issuing admin; enrollment with East course; bulk operation with East admin or East course; audit event with East actor_admin_id.
findings.suggestedFix: Add UNIQUE (id, tenant_id) to certificates, enrollments and bulk_issue_operations and make the four references composite, or reword the README sentence.

findings.title: A write request waiting for SQLite's write lock freezes the whole server process for up to 10 s; replays and 409s of already-stored keys get 503 meanwhile
findings.description: Every write path, including the idempotency lookup that only serves a replay or a 409, starts with a synchronous BEGIN IMMEDIATE on the server's single connection, which has busy_timeout = 10,000 ms. When another process holds the write lock (the generator CLI, which the README and the script header say can run while the server is up; a second server process in a long bulk issue; db:reset), SQLite's busy handler sleeps on Node's main thread. During that wait the process answers no other request (measured with certificate list requests), and after 10 s the write fails with 503 database_busy and Retry-After: 1. A client that follows Retry-After freezes the process for another 10 s per attempt, so list requests are effectively unavailable for as long as the other writer runs. Requests sent on an already-open keep-alive connection during the freeze are dropped with a connection reset when it ends. For A2/A3 the effect is availability only: a retry of a key whose result is already stored gets 503 instead of the stored 201, a misuse gets 503 instead of 409, and in a two-process setup an identical concurrent request on the other process gets 503 when the operation runs longer than 10 s. I saw no double execution, partial write or wrong replay in any of these runs; once the lock is free the retry behaves correctly. With the documented default of 100,000 rows the stall is about 2.4 s and nothing fails.
findings.expected: README.md:102 and backend/scripts/generate-certificates.js:10 say the generator can run while the server is up, and README.md:213 says 'readers never block the writer and the writer never blocks readers'. A waiting writer should not stop the process from answering reads, and a replay or 409 for a key that is already stored should not need the write lock.
findings.reproduction:
In a copy of the project (API only):
  PORT=4205 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=/abs/x.sqlite node backend/src/server.js &
  (cd backend && node scripts/generate-certificates.js --db /abs/x.sqlite --count 600000) &   # 26.9 s here
  sleep 1
  curl -s -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' -X POST -H 'X-Actor-Email: alice@east.test' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: k1' -d '{"courseId":1}' http://127.0.0.1:4205/api/bulk-issues &
  sleep 0.5
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' -H 'X-Actor-Email: alice@east.test' 'http://127.0.0.1:4205/api/certificates?pageSize=5'
Observed: baseline list 0.007 s. Bulk issue: HTTP 503 {"error":{"code":"database_busy",...}} after 10.02 s with Retry-After: 1. The list request sent 0.5 s later: HTTP 200 after 9.53 s. After the generator finished the same key returned 201 replayed=false once, then replayed=true.
Other measurements (scripts t_longwriter.mjs, t_keepalive.mjs, t_bigop.mjs in my work/scripts directory):
- Default generator, 100,000 rows (2.6 s): bulk issue 201 after 2,449 ms; list requests sent meanwhile took up to 2,353 ms (normally about 5 ms).
- 1,000,000 rows (52.8 s), client honouring Retry-After: four consecutive 503s after 10.02-10.03 s each, then 201. Of 530 list requests sent every 100 ms: median 2.0 s, p90 6.4 s, max 9.8 s, 108 slower than 5 s, several failed with 'read ECONNRESET'.
- Key already stored (201), then the generator started: replay of the same key returned 503 after 10.02 s; the same key with another course returned 503 after 10.02 s instead of 409; GET /api/bulk-issues/1 at the same moment returned 200 in 2 ms.
- Keep-alive: a list request on a previously used keep-alive socket, sent 1 s into the wait, ended in ECONNRESET; the same request on a new connection got 200 after 9,033 ms.
- Two server processes, 300,000-learner bulk issue on A (14.4 s): the identical request on B got 503 after 10,040 ms and the stored body on retry; a list request on B took 10,064 ms.
findings.suggestedFix: Answer replays and 409s from a plain read first and take the write lock only when the key is unknown (re-checking under the lock). Use a short busy_timeout (about 100-250 ms) and retry BEGIN IMMEDIATE asynchronously with back-off up to the same 10 s budget so the event loop keeps serving reads, or run writes on a worker thread. Optionally let the generator commit in batches.

findings.title: Reusing a key with a payload the JSON parser rejects returns 400 / 413 / 415 instead of 409
findings.description: The body is parsed by express.json (strict mode, 100 kB limit) before the route looks at the Idempotency-Key. When Alice reuses a key that already executed with malformed JSON, with valid JSON that is not an object or array (null, 1, "1"), with a body over 100 kB or with an unsupported charset or content encoding, the answer is 400 invalid_json, 413 payload_too_large or 415, not 409. This conflicts with the wording of A3: "If Alice reuses an `Idempotency-Key` with a different course ID or payload, return `409 Conflict` without executing a second operation or overwriting the first result." The safety half of the sentence holds: nothing was executed and the stored result was untouched (hash over all rows identical before and after each request). Only the status code deviates. Every changed payload that does parse (other course, extra field, other value type, {}, [1], empty or missing body) correctly returned 409. For null, 1 and "1" the message 'Request body is not valid JSON' is also inaccurate, since these are valid JSON documents.
findings.expected: A3 as written: 409 Conflict for any reuse of the key with a different payload. If 400 for unparseable bodies is the intended behaviour, the README should say so.
findings.reproduction:
A='X-Actor-Email: alice@east.test'; U=http://127.0.0.1:4201/api/bulk-issues  (fresh database)
  curl -s -X POST -H "$A" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: K1' -d '{"courseId":1}' $U     -> 201, 2 issued
  same key, -d '{oops'             -> 400 invalid_json
  same key, -d '{"courseId":1'     -> 400 invalid_json
  same key, -d '{"courseId":1}x'   -> 400 invalid_json
  same key, -d 'null' / '1' / '"1"' -> 400 invalid_json ("Request body is not valid JSON")
  same key, 120 kB body {"courseId":1,"pad":"xxx..."} -> 413 payload_too_large
  same key, Content-Type: application/json; charset=latin1 -> 415 invalid_request
  same key, Content-Encoding: zstd-unknown -> 415
For comparison, same key with -d '{"courseId":2}', '{}', '[1]', empty body -> 409 idempotency_key_reused.
After all of these the hash over every row of all tables was unchanged and an honest retry returned the first body (script t_misuse.mjs in my work/scripts directory).
findings.suggestedFix: For POST /api/bulk-issues, look the key up before (or independently of) body parsing: if the (tenant, admin, key) record exists and the body cannot be parsed or fingerprinted, answer 409 idempotency_key_reused. Alternatively document that unparseable bodies are always 400/413/415.

findings.title: Deeply nested JSON body overflows the stack in the request fingerprint: 500 instead of 409 or replay, and an identical retry can get 500 where the first attempt got 201
findings.description: canonicalJson() recurses once per nesting level and is called for every bulk-issue request before the transaction starts. A body nested a few thousand levels deep (about 6 kB, well under the 100 kB limit) makes it throw RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which the error handler turns into 500 internal_error. Consequences: (1) a reused key with such a payload gets 500, not 409; (2) the depth at which it fails depends on the JIT state of the process, so the same key and body can execute once (201) and then be answered with 500 on an honest retry after a restart, instead of the stored response; (3) the UI and any well-behaved client treat 5xx as retryable. The overflow happens before BEGIN, so nothing is written and the connection stays healthy; the stored result remains available via GET /api/bulk-issues/:id. The console's own UI never sends such bodies.
findings.expected: A client-controlled payload should produce a 4xx (or be fingerprinted without recursion), and an identical retry of an executed request should receive the stored response (A2: 'All callers receive the same logical outcome').
findings.reproduction:
python3 -c "d=3000; print('{\"courseId\":1,\"x\":' + '['*d + ']'*d + '}', end='')" > deep.json     # 6,019 bytes
curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Actor-Email: alice@east.test' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: seq-1' --data-binary @deep.json http://127.0.0.1:4200/api/bulk-issues
(seq-1 had already executed for {"courseId":1}; expected 409)
-> HTTP 500 {"error":{"code":"internal_error","message":"Unexpected server error"}}; the same body without a key -> 500.
Server log: [error] POST /api/bulk-issues: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded at canonicalJson (backend/src/lib/fingerprint.js:6:46).
Threshold (script t_deep.mjs, fresh keys): freshly started server: depth 1000/2000/2500 -> 201, 3000 -> 500, 3500 -> 500, 4000 -> 201, 5000 -> 500; after 300 warm-up requests: 3000-6000 -> 201, 8000 -> 500.
Inconsistent retry: on the warmed-up server, key flaky-1 with the depth-3000 body -> 201 replayed=false (2 issued). After restarting the server, six identical retries (same key, same body) -> 500 internal_error each; database unchanged.
findings.suggestedFix: Make canonicalJson iterative or enforce a maximum nesting depth (reject deeper bodies with 400), and catch RangeError around the fingerprint so it maps to a 4xx.

findings.title: The cross-process A2 test does not exercise a cross-process race: the suite still passes with the idempotency lookup moved outside the write transaction
findings.description: README.md:198 lists 'two server processes on one database' as the verification that identical requests are serialised across processes. In the test, 20 requests alternate between a server that is already warm from the previous test and one that has just been spawned, so the two processes' transactions practically never overlap. I applied the classic check-then-act regression to a separate copy (idempotency lookup done before db.transaction, everything else unchanged): the A2+A3 group passed 20 of 20 runs and the unit plus acceptance files passed 8 of 8 runs (67 tests each). The same mutated code fails immediately under a real overlap: my two-process harness saw an HTTP 500 (UNIQUE violation on idx_bulk_ops_idempotency) in 142 of 150 rounds. A second mutation (bulk-issue transaction opened with deferred BEGIN instead of BEGIN IMMEDIATE) passed the group 6 of 6 times and was caught in only 10 of 30 runs when the cross-process test ran in isolation. The single-process '25 simultaneous requests' test cannot detect ordering defects by construction because the server is synchronous. The shipped product code is correct here; the finding is that this guard would not notice if it stopped being so.
findings.expected: A test that claims to guard cross-process serialisation should fail reliably when the lookup is no longer performed under the write lock.
findings.reproduction:
In a separate copy of backend/ (never the original): in src/services/bulkIssue.js move the block '1. Idempotency lookup' (lines 65-86) out of the db.transaction callback so it runs before 'return db.transaction(() => {'. Then:
  for i in $(seq 1 20); do node --test --test-concurrency=1 --test-name-pattern='A2|A3' test/acceptance.test.js | grep '^ℹ fail'; done      -> 'fail 0' 20 times
  node --test --test-concurrency=1 test/unit.test.js test/acceptance.test.js    (8 runs) -> tests 67, pass 67, fail 0 each time
My harness against the same mutated copy (two servers on one DB, 150 rounds of 16 simultaneous identical requests with a fresh key per round): 142 rounds contained a 500, e.g. round 0: 1x 201 replayed=false, 14x 201 replayed=true, 1x 500. Against the unmodified code the same harness reports 0 anomalies.
Second mutation (append ', { immediate: false }' to the outer db.transaction call in bulkIssue): A2|A3 group passed 6 of 6; the test 'holds across processes' run in isolation failed in 10 of 30 runs.
findings.suggestedFix: Force the overlap deterministically: hold the write lock from a helper connection (BEGIN IMMEDIATE), send the same request to both server processes, wait until both are blocked, then COMMIT and assert one execution plus one replay. Alternatively loop the two-process race over many fresh keys with both servers warmed up.

findings.title: Two processes started at the same time on a new database file: one of them crashes during initialisation
findings.description: Schema creation and seeding are check-then-act: migrate() reads PRAGMA user_version and openInitializedDatabase() calls isSeeded() outside the transaction that then creates the schema or inserts the demo data. When two processes (two servers, or a server and the generator or init CLI) open a database file that does not exist yet at the same moment, both decide to initialise; the second one to get the write lock fails and exits with code 1. The database itself ends up seeded exactly once and consistent, and starting the failed process again works. This matters only for multi-process use, which the README advertises ('cross-process correctness') but the single-command quick start does not need.
findings.expected: Initialisation should be safe to race: re-check user_version and isSeeded inside the BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction and treat 'already initialised' as success.
findings.reproduction:
DB=/abs/new.sqlite   (file does not exist)
  PORT=4206 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=$DB node backend/src/server.js &
  PORT=4207 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=$DB node backend/src/server.js &
Observed: the first process logs 'Created demo data' and listens; the second exits with code 1:
  SqliteError: table tenants already exists
    at Connection.exec (backend/src/db/sqlite.js:105:15)
    at backend/src/db/schema.js:162:8 ... at migrate (schema.js:161:6) at openInitializedDatabase (bootstrap.js:9:5)
Loop (script t_startrace.mjs, 10 rounds of 2 simultaneous starts on a fresh file): one process died in each of the 10 rounds, 9 times with 'Error: Database already contains data; refusing to seed twice' and once with 'SqliteError: table tenants already exists'. The resulting database had 11 certificates and 13 audit events, i.e. seeded once.
findings.suggestedFix: Inside the migration transaction re-read user_version and return if it is already current; inside seedDemoData return (instead of throwing) when isSeeded() is true.

findings.title: db:reset deletes the live database files when it cannot get the write lock within 10 s; the running server keeps working on the unlinked file and acknowledged operations vanish on restart
findings.description: Outside my assigned area, found while testing long-running writers. init-db.js --reset first tries an in-place reset in one transaction; if that throws for any reason it falls back to deleting the database, -wal and -shm files and creating a new database. One such reason is SQLITE_BUSY after the 10 s busy timeout, which happens whenever another process holds the write lock that long (a generator run of a few hundred thousand rows, or a very large bulk issue). The files are then unlinked underneath the processes that still have them open. The reset reports success with exit code 0, the still-running generator also reports success but wrote into the deleted file, and the running server keeps serving and writing the deleted file while the path now holds a different database. A bulk issue acknowledged with 201 through that server is not in the database on disk; after a server restart the operation, its certificates, its audit events and its idempotency record are gone and the same key executes again as a new operation. The README calls the command safe while the server is running. With an idle server the in-place path works correctly (verified: same inode, server sees fresh data, later writes persist). I rated this minor because the trigger is narrow and the command's purpose is to discard data, but the failure is silent.
findings.expected: README.md:42 'Restores the pristine quick-start dataset (safe while the server is running)', README.md:287 '(works while the server runs)', and the init-db.js header comment 'it is safe even while the server is running'. A reset that cannot obtain the lock should fail or wait, never remove files other processes have open.
findings.reproduction:
Script t_reset.mjs in my work/scripts directory; equivalent commands in a copy:
  PORT=4201 DB_PATH=/abs/r.sqlite node backend/src/server.js &
  (cd backend && node scripts/generate-certificates.js --db /abs/r.sqlite --count 700000) &      # holds the write lock about 27 s
  sleep 1.5; (cd backend && node scripts/init-db.js --reset --db /abs/r.sqlite)
Observed:
  reset exited with code 0 after about 10 s, printing 'In-place reset was not possible (database is locked); recreating the database file.' then 'Database ready ...: 2 tenants, 6 courses, 13 learners, 11 certificates.'
  generator exited with code 0: 'Tenant East now has 700,007 certificates in total.'
  inode of the database file changed from 648991 to 649002
  running server: GET /api/certificates total = 700007; database file on disk: 11 certificates, 0 operations
  POST /api/bulk-issues through the running server (key after-reset, course 1) -> 201, 2 issued; database file on disk still 11 certificates, 0 operations
  after restarting the server: GET /api/bulk-issues lists 0 operations; the same key -> 201 replayed=false with a new createdAt, i.e. it executed again.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the delete-and-recreate fallback for lock errors: on SQLITE_BUSY print 'database is busy, try again' and exit non-zero, or keep waiting. Recreate the file only when it is not a usable database, and document that the server must be stopped in that case.

findings.title: Starting on a port that is already in use ends in a TypeError stack trace instead of the intended 'Port ... is already in use' message
findings.description: Outside my assigned area, hit by accident. Express 5's app.listen registers the listen callback as a one-time 'error' listener as well (node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-606, version 5.3.0). On EADDRINUSE the callback in server.js therefore runs first, calls server.address(), which is null, and throws. The process dies with an uncaught TypeError and the friendly handler a few lines below never prints its message. The exit code is still 1, so only the diagnostic is wrong, but a busy default port is the most likely first-run problem and the README troubleshooting section covers it.
findings.expected: The message coded at server.js:33: 'Port <n> is already in use. Stop the other process or run with PORT=<free port>.' (README.md:286 lists this case under Troubleshooting).
findings.reproduction:
With a server already listening on 4200:
  PORT=4200 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=/abs/other.sqlite node backend/src/server.js
Observed (exit code 1):
  backend/src/server.js:22
    const { port } = server.address();
  TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'port' of 'server.address(...)' as it is null.
      at Server.<anonymous> (backend/src/server.js:22:11)
      at Server.f (node_modules/once/once.js:25:25) ... at emitErrorNT (node:net:1977:8)
The text 'Port 4200 is already in use' never appears.
findings.suggestedFix: Give the listen callback an error parameter and handle it there (if (err) { print the port message; process.exit(1) }), or create the server with http.createServer(app) and attach the 'error' handler before calling listen.
